clinical_knowledge.topic: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: facial rash, joint pain, hair loss, and fatigue worsening over 3 months
Key HPI features: 29F presents with 3 months of worsening fatigue, pain in hand and wrist joints, increased hair shedding, and a red rash across her cheeks and nose that flares up after sun exposure.
Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Dermatomyositis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Foamy urine or swelling — kidney involvement.
management_principles: Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
: Check ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith antibodies, complement levels, and urinalysis (to screen for lupus nephritis)

Prompt rheumatology-directed management is required; emergency assessment is needed for nephritis, neurologic symptoms, chest pain/dyspnea, severe cytopenia symptoms, or other organ-threatening disease.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
reference_soap.plan: Confirm the syndrome with targeted testing rather than ANA alone: CBC, creatinine/eGFR, urinalysis with microscopy and urine protein quantification, complements, anti-dsDNA, and other serology as clinically indicated. Urgent same-day assessment is needed for reduced urine output, edema/foamy urine, hypertension, neurologic symptoms, chest pain/dyspnea, or severe illness. Rheumatology should direct hydroxychloroquine, glucocorticoids, or immunosuppressants with pregnancy planning, eye screening, infection review, and laboratory monitoring.

teaching.one_liner: A multisystem autoimmune disease causing a sun-sensitive facial rash, joint pain, hair loss, and fatigue — needs screening for internal organ, especially kidney, involvement.
red_flags: Foamy urine or swelling — kidney involvement
